section: Research is more than collecting quotations
assessment: The notes define research through systematic inquiry, novelty, reliable knowledge and practical significance. Their Tuckman and Popper references are incomplete edition-level citations, not authenticated quotations here. Falsifiability and criticism concern how claims can be challenged; no research method guarantees final true statements. The reference to the UK REF is a contextual example, not a universal requirement for every project.

Basic and applied objectives can overlap. Discovering something unknown to you does not alone show it is new to the field. Novel data, combinations, methods or applications need an argument for what they add. The history-of-universities comments are supplied context, not independently established historical findings.

section: Systematic does not automatically mean unbiased
assessment: A documented design makes choices open to scrutiny. Induction/deduction, evidence and philosophical argument can contribute in different ways; generalization is not necessarily statistical. Replicability requires sufficiently documented procedures and materials where appropriate. Reflect on researcher involvement, assumptions, sampling and instrument wording rather than treating an orderly process as proof of objectivity.

section: A research cycle and a practical start
assessment: The supplied cycle links a field/debate, literature, question, design, data, interpretation and impact. Begin early enough to obtain access, receive feedback and change direction when evidence requires it.

The source’s first rows use item/element/purpose labels. Later measurement and analysis prompts do not fit that grid perfectly; their wording is retained rather than silently rewritten as a required institutional template.

section: Quantitative design: common patterns, not guarantees
assessment: Quantitative work often uses numerical measurements and specified models, but it is not automatically deductive, objective, random or generalizable. The source’s minimum of 80 per subgroup is not a universal reliability requirement. Sample justification must address design, precision or power, effects, variation, analysis and feasibility. The five stages are useful prompts, not a guarantee that a research question is already a statistical hypothesis.

Researcher distance, predetermined structure, random samples and numerical data are tendencies in this teaching contrast, not necessary properties of every quantitative study. Reliability is a property to assess, not something implied by numbers or described as “hard” data.

section: Qualitative design and the scope of interpretation
assessment: Qualitative inquiry can be inductive, deductive or combine reasoning. It does not have a universal maximum participant count. Purposive depth and contextual understanding differ from statistical population estimation; transferability or analytic generalization needs its own argument. The source’s small-sample-to-wider-sample statement is too broad. One research question can help focus a project, but is not a universal rule.

section: Philosophical assumptions and forms of evidence
assessment: Words, images, records and observations can be qualitative material, but data format alone does not define the research design. Ontology, epistemology and methodology address different questions. Social construction and researcher involvement describe some perspectives; they do not exhaust phenomenology or all qualitative traditions. Flexible design still needs justified choices and systematic analysis.

Exploratory work can inform a survey, while survey results can guide follow-up interviews. Explain how and why the strands are integrated; simply collecting two types of data does not make their inferences coherent. Induction/deduction are reasoning approaches, not synonyms for qualitative/quantitative data.

section: Four concerns that must not be collapsed
assessment: Operationalization connects a concept with indicators or observations. Reliability concerns consistency under specified conditions; validity concerns the interpretation and use of the evidence. The notes imply greater reliability resolves causal interpretation, but causal identification also needs a defensible design and assumptions. Population inference depends on the target, sampling and response process; random sampling alone does not guarantee generalizability. Replication needs transparent materials and procedures, not identical results promised in advance.

The source lists external audit, peer debriefing, bias clarification, engagement, rich description, triangulation, member checking and discrepant information. These can serve different purposes; not all are mandatory or suitable in every interpretive tradition. Explain what each contributes and how disagreement is treated.

The notes identify observation, diaries, interviews, field-note forms and secondary records. Assess authenticity, credibility, representativeness and meaning. Public availability is not proof of accuracy; private access is not unrestricted permission to publish.

Basic, explanatory, focused and silent probes can elicit different information. Drawing out, mirroring and laddering need care: offering ideas can lead an answer. Avoid ambiguity, double questions, leading language and unexplained terms; sometimes a defined technical term is needed, rather than banned altogether.

Case study, grounded theory, ethnography, action research, observation, focus groups, interviews, diaries and historical/archive work operate at different levels of design and collection. Choose a coherent combination rather than treating every list item as an interchangeable method.

section: Quantitative pros and cons: preserve the claims, assess the conditions
assessment:
These claims mix study design, cost, response, objectivity, generalization, anonymity and software convenience. None follows simply from choosing quantitative data. The assertion that subjects are not influenced by observation conflicts with common measurement/reactivity problems; software does not guarantee validity or rapid analysis. A structured interview can include follow-up questions.
Several in-text references are incomplete or identify web/practitioner material rather than a specified scholarly article. Names such as “LG,” “Natasha,” a journal title/year, or a misspelled author/year cannot be reliably matched by guessing. The catalogue covers the supplied workbook; these handout citations remain visible here with their original claims until their actual sources are identified.

section: Qualitative pros and cons: distinguish interpretation from stereotypes
assessment: The list includes plausible concerns about skill, context and sampling, but also misfiled claims about large samples/objectivity and statistical assumptions. Qualitative findings are not merely unconstrained “gut feel.” Conversely, a detailed account is not automatically causal evidence or statistically representative. Preserve the source attributions, but do not use a blog-style advantages list or an incomplete author/year as proof of universal methodological superiority.

The source contains four unavailable-download placeholders. No underlying text, image or attachment identifies what they contained. They are mapped and retained as missing material, not counted as successfully recovered knowledge. No replacement content is invented.

section: Question, access and the meaning of theory
assessment: The source asks about a debate, available evidence and access, then gives several senses of theory. Specify which concepts, explanations or propositions the project actually uses; do not treat a dictionary-like list as a complete account of scientific theory.

The contrast between theory and practice is useful, but the source overstates universal requirements. Not every dissertation must collect new data from businesses; conceptual, secondary-data and other designs can be legitimate when the programme and question allow them. Start from a problem and relevant debate, refine scope through reading and assess access before committing. Novelty cannot be established merely by avoiding a frequently studied topic.

Map the field, extract concepts/arguments/methods into a literature matrix, critique the evidence and write the synthesis. The source repeats the planning-the-review line; the original positions remain mapped. “Incomplete, incommensurable, inadequate” are critique prompts, not conclusions to assign without explanation.

The source connects positioning and argument, literature, model/hypotheses, design and measurement, results, interpretation and limitations. Attitude, subjective norm, perceived control and intention are named as a short conceptual example without an attributed model or dataset; no empirical results are supplied.

The source emphasizes question/literature, context and observation procedures, qualitative patterns, interpretation, practice, propositions and future inquiry. This is a possible structure, not an institution-wide required format.

The TIP list suggests possible paper contexts—change, crisis/continuity, digital transformation, work ethics, upgrading and lived cases. These are topic prompts, not developed research findings or separate complete subjects to publish as new lessons.

section: Paraphrase and quotation: attribution plus accurate locators
assessment: Paraphrased ideas still need attribution; exact quotations need accurate wording and a page or other locator where available. The Robson/Robson, Burn/Brunt and CIPD examples are supplied teaching examples whose exact publications and quotations have not been authenticated. Single versus double quotation marks and page syntax depend on the required style; they are not universal rules.

The source distinguishes works cited from a broader bibliography and gives book, article, online-article and website templates. Keep versions, dates, authors, pages and DOI/URLs identifiable. Publisher location and access-date conventions vary across styles; do not silently present one old template as every institution’s rule.

section: Choose sources by evidence, not domain suffix
assessment: Scholarly, professional, government and popular material serve different purposes. A .edu/.ac/.gov/.org address is not by itself proof that a particular claim is reliable; neither does a commercial domain disqualify a journal publisher. Wikipedia can help discover leads but is not a substitute for the underlying work. Google Scholar indexes material; it is not the author or publisher of everything it finds. Distinguish databases, search services, journal platforms and the works retrieved.

Strategic and operational consultancy can use research, benchmarking and existing knowledge in different ways. The source’s statements about what every applied study “needs” and the history of MBA strategy modules are supplied assertions, not universal requirements or independently verified history.

section: Case study and action research: a useful but simplified contrast
assessment: The source contrasts observing/reporting with intervening/learning. A case study need not always involve total researcher independence or only external knowledge contributions; action research requires systematic reflection on participation, intervention and evidence, not simply taking action. Explain boundaries, influence, ethical responsibilities and the risk that an intervention fails.

Connect what/why/how/when, intended effects, priorities, milestones, ownership and implementation resources to the evidence. A promised improvement in profit, speed, retention or wellbeing remains a proposition to assess, not a guaranteed consequence of the research.

section: Target population, frame and random selection
assessment: Distinguish whom you want to describe, whom you can reach, the sampling frame and the actual participants. Random sampling concerns selection; random assignment concerns treatment allocation and supports different arguments.

For a simple equal-probability systematic design, sampling fraction f = n/N and selection interval k = N/n are different quantities. Use a justified random start and handle non-integer intervals and frame periodicity appropriately rather than following the source’s fraction wording literally. Stratification divides the frame into relevant groups before selection; document allocation and weights where needed.

section: Quota, convenience, purposive and network recruitment
assessment: Quota sampling can match selected proportions without random within-quota selection. Convenience selects accessibility; purposive sampling selects for an analytic purpose and should not be collapsed into the same definition. Snowball recruitment can aid access but depends on starting points and networks; the Bryman example has only an abbreviated reference.

section: Justify sample size for the design
assessment: Time, cost, precision/power, heterogeneity, response and intended analysis matter. The n=1000 example is not a universal stopping point, and the Hazelrigg reference is incomplete. Random or nominally representative selection does not automatically permit an arbitrarily small sample. Complex models and small cells need design-specific assessment rather than a blanket rule.

Distinguish random sampling error, coverage/non-response, instrument/collection and processing errors. Wording, fatigue, missing data, literacy/access and uncertainty about who responded can affect findings. Some listed limitations apply to a particular self-administered questionnaire, not every survey design.

Nominal variables label categories; counts are summaries of observations in those categories, not the definition of nominal measurement. Ordinal values express order without guaranteed equal spacing. Interval scales support meaningful equal differences; ratio scales also have a meaningful zero. Height and counts are typically ratio examples, so the source’s “interval” list conflates them with the software’s broad Scale classification.

section: Discrete/continuous and level of measurement are different
assessment: Discrete/continuous describes possible values or measurement practice; nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio concerns meaning and permitted comparisons. Celsius versus Kelvin temperature illustrates why the unit matters. Income, age, IQ and education need operational definitions and context. Gender and religion categories should suit the question and participants rather than assume one universal coding scheme.

Open/closed, dichotomous/multiple-category, frequency, ranking, Likert, graphical, semantic differential and nonverbal formats offer different response tasks. A single Likert item and a justified multi-item scale are not automatically interchangeable. “Seminar activities” has no supplied exercise or dataset.

section: Association is more than “describing a relationship”
assessment: Pearson correlation describes linear association under appropriate measurement and inferential conditions; Spearman uses ranks to assess monotonic association. Regression models a specified outcome given predictors and assumptions. All describe relationships in different senses; the source’s distinction is not valid. Identify dependence, outliers and the intended estimand before choosing.

Paired t analysis concerns within-pair differences under its conditions; repeated-measures ANOVA models a specified repeated design and additional covariance/sphericity considerations. A paired sign test is not an independent two-sample test; Friedman is a related-samples rank procedure for suitable designs. These are possible tools, not every analysis of two versus three measurements.

section: Independent groups, factors, covariates and counts
assessment: A two-group mean comparison needs assumptions and an appropriate variance approach; do not assume a pooled-variance Student test is always suitable. One-way versus factorial ANOVA depends on the number of factors and design, not merely the number of groups. Ordinary ANCOVA is a model with covariates, not a nonparametric fallback alongside Mann–Whitney. Rank tests do not remove independence or design requirements; Mann–Whitney does not universally test a difference in medians without further conditions. Chi-square procedures concern appropriate categorical counts with expected-frequency/design conditions.

section: What the output families can and cannot tell you
assessment: Frequencies, descriptive summaries, crosstabs, correlations, mean comparisons and regression answer different questions. A significance test does not establish a probability that a relationship exists, and regression is more than “correlation plus a constant.” Assess assumptions, estimates, uncertainty and the design. The menu terminology is an undated study note, not verified instructions for an installed version.

Counts, percentages, missingness, central tendency and dispersion provide context. Record coding, the denominator and the population/sample each table describes; a crosstab alone does not establish causation.

section: Null, alternative and the question actually tested
assessment: A null is a specified hypothesis within a test/model; it is not necessarily a status quo held until proven false. The alternative must correspond to the estimand and design. The attendance example shifts from association to a positive causal effect; observational association alone does not justify that causal wording. Report estimates and uncertainty as well as a decision threshold.

Specify direction and analysis before observing results when using confirmatory tests. A directional scientific claim is different from choosing a test tail after seeing the data. Whether a statistic has a one-sided rejection region does not automatically make the scientific alternative directional; the source’s “one side impossible” shortcut is insufficient. The wage and promotional-email examples are teaching hypotheses, not supplied findings.
